title: When To Reteach Your Classroom Rules
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes between two situations that look similar but call for very different responses. Ordinary "testing" of newly taught rules — a student breaking a rule shortly after it's introduced — is normal and should be handled with calm, immediate, consistent follow-through, not reteaching; he compares the ideal response to an NFL referee calling what he sees with no hesitation or negotiation. Daily review of the plan in the first days of school is treated as a separate, non-reactive category that helps limit testing generally. The more serious scenario, and his central diagnostic claim, is when several students misbehave at once or in quick succession — a sign the plan wasn't taught with enough clarity or that the class has already concluded the teacher is a pushover. In that specific case, he argues a teacher must stop the lesson entirely and reteach the plan immediately with doubled modeling, explicitness, and practice. The concrete takeaway is that consistent enforcement resolves ordinary testing, while only a genuine multi-student breakdown justifies interrupting instruction to reteach.
points: Isolated rule-testing after a rule is introduced calls for calm, consistent enforcement — not reteaching.
Consistent follow-through is said to make testing stop "every single time" once students see a teacher is fully committed.
Multiple students misbehaving at once or in succession is treated as a distinct red flag that the plan wasn't taught clearly enough.
In that specific multi-student scenario, the recommended response is to stop the lesson and reteach with doubled modeling and practice.
quotes: One follows the other like the forming and crashing of a North Shore wave. No hesitating. No reminding. No negotiating.
Once you prove that you’re all-in committed, the testing will stop. Every. Single. Time.
It’s when more than a small few students are misbehaving at the same time.
Either way, they’re misbehaving because they believe you’re a pushover.
Reteach it with double the modeling, double the explicitness, and double the practice. Hammer it home.
